newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER SHOWCASE-FIERY WELSH DRAGONS MELLOW WITH AGE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-FIERY WELSH DRAGONS MELLOW WITH AGE.

text.p: Wimbledon's Vinnie Jones and Chelsea's Mark Hughes are a pair of Welsh dragons who can breathe fire and terrify opponents like few other men in British soccer.
But as they prepare for Sunday's all-London F.A. Cup semifinal at Highbury, the 30-somethings with the ferocious tempers appear to be mellowing with age.
Hughes, playing the best football of his career at Chelsea, has discovered a serene side to his nature which was seldom evident during his years at Manchester United.

And while the combative centre-forward has reaped the benefits of self-control, his Wales team mate Jones has mastered the art of ball control, defying the critics who claimed he was nothing but a kick-and-rush man.
Vinnie Jones is one of a rare breed of footballers who seems to have lived a dozen lives by the age of 30.
A chat show host, sometime male model, newspaper contributor and self-styled land-owning gent, he has dabbled in Oxford University debates and appeared at a United Nations conference on human rights.
He says his latest ambitions are to appear in a film and become "England's answer to Jean Marc Bosman" by challenging anomalies in the domestic transfer system.
But above all, Jones is Wimbledon Football Club.

In the 11 years since he joined the club from minor league Wealdstone for just 10,000 pounds ($16,200), the big midfielder with the square chin and close-cropped hair has become a talisman for the club.
He won the F.A. Cup final with Wimbledon in 1988 and, after a spell at several other clubs including Chelsea, he returned in 1992 as a prodigal son to the place where he first made his name.
He is famous for being sent off and once got himself booked for a brutal challenge five seconds into a match.
He also appeared in a tongue-in-cheek video on how to hack down opponents, a move which earned him a 20,000 pound ($32,400) fine and a great deal of embarrassment.
But Jones is a sentimentalist too.
When he was given the captaincy of his adopted nation, the man with a Welsh dragon tattooed across his broad chest was reportedly on the verge of tears.

"Wimbledon play with 10 men and Vinnie Jones," the club's owner Sam Hammam said. "In many respects they are ahead of him from a technical and footballing angle but what Vinnie provides is leadership."
Jones, like the Wimbledon side he personifies, has developed his game beyond recognition this season.

"Maybe it's taken me 10 years to learn that it doesn't matter how much you roar about and give 110 percent," he said in a recent interview. "If you pass the ball to your own team three or four times you get more recognition."
On Sunday Jones will tackle Hughes, an equally fierce competitor who has also fine-tuned his game in recent years.

Known at Stamford Bridge as "Popeye" after the spinach-eating cartoon sailor with the strength of an ox, Hughes still frightens the life out of defenders and acts as a perfect counter-balance to little Gianfranco Zola in the Chelsea attack.
"I have played with some very good forwards," Zola said recently. "Alessandro Del Piero, Fabrizio Ravanelli, Gigi Casiraghi,... but I rate Mark just as highly."
"Mark is a very serious man, very quiet. It is easy to see that he is a very intelligent person and that comes across on the pitch."

Hughes, who had spells at Barcelona and Bayern Munich before returning to the hustle and bustle of the English game, acknowledges he has mellowed since his early days at United when he was constantly in trouble with both referees and opponents.
The fire which has earned him over 60 Welsh caps burns no less brightly, but he now compliments it with quick thinking and wonderful ball control.
"In the last five or six seasons I have learned as much as in the rest of my career put together," he says. "That is because of the quality of players I have been fortunate to work with."
"I realise that for 10 or 15 years I wasted so much energy racing around trying to kick people because they had kicked me...I am more into energy conservation these days."
